nameStory: The Arctic Paperbubble gets its name from its delicate, translucent shell that's so thin it looks like it could be made of tissue paper formed into a tiny bubble. The 'Arctic' part reflects its love of cold northern waters, where it thrives in the chilly conditions that would send many other sea snails packing.
description: The Arctic Paperbubble is a tiny marine snail with an incredibly delicate, almost transparent shell that you can practically see through like a soap bubble. This miniature mollusk is one of the smaller sea snails you'll encounter along New England's coast, small enough that you might mistake it for a droplet of water at first glance. Despite its fragile appearance, this little gastropod is surprisingly hardy, making its home in the challenging conditions of the intertidal zone. It belongs to a group of sea snails known for their paper-thin shells and ability to thrive in cold waters.

idTips.label: Shell transparency
idTips.description: The shell is remarkably thin and translucent, like frosted glass or a soap bubble - you can often see the animal's body through it when held up to light

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Extremely small, easily overlooked among beach debris - smaller than most other sea snails you'll find washed up

idTips.label: Shell texture
idTips.description: Feels incredibly fragile when handled, almost like touching a piece of thin plastic wrap - handle with extreme care

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Shell appears whitish to pale yellow, sometimes with a slight pearlescent sheen that catches the light

idTips.label: Shape
idTips.description: Rounded and bubble-like rather than the spiral tower shape of many snails, with a relatively large opening

habitat: Look for Arctic Paperbubbles in the intertidal zone along New England's rocky coasts, particularly in tide pools and among seaweed beds where they can find shelter from crashing waves. They prefer the colder waters of northern New England, doing especially well in areas with good water circulation and rocky substrates that provide plenty of nooks and crannies.

seasonality.spring: Most active as waters begin to warm, though still quite cold. Look for them in shallow tide pools during low spring tides when they're easier to spot.
seasonality.summer: Can be found year-round but may be less active during the warmest summer months. Check early morning tide pools when water temperatures are coolest.
seasonality.fall: Often easier to observe as cooler temperatures return and they become more active. Good time to search tide pools after storms.
seasonality.winter: Most active season due to cold water preferences, though harsh winter storms may make coastal observation challenging.

funFact: Despite having one of the most fragile shells in the ocean, Arctic Paperbubbles are actually circumpolar - meaning they've managed to spread all the way around the Arctic Ocean, from New England to Europe to Alaska, somehow surviving epic journeys across some of the world's roughest seas with their tissue-paper armor!
confusionNotes: Could be mistaken for juvenile moon snails or other small gastropods, but the Arctic Paperbubble's extreme shell transparency is unique - if you can see through it like a window, you've likely found your paperbubble. Remember: most other small snails have opaque shells you can't see through.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'paperbubble' perfectly captures what makes this species special - it's essentially evolution's experiment in making the thinnest possible shell that still works, like nature's version of tissue paper that somehow doesn't dissolve in saltwater.
compareHints: Since it's the only Diaphana species commonly found in New England, compare it to other bubble snails in the same order (Cephalaspidea). Arctic Paperbubbles are distinguished by their extreme shell transparency and smaller size compared to most other bubble snails. While other bubble snails may have thin shells, none approach the glass-like clarity of the Arctic Paperbubble's shell.
